newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: French strike may make Portuguese truckers go bust.
newsitem.headline: French strike may make Portuguese truckers go bust.

text.p: Portuguese road transport companies could go bankrupt if the French truckers' strike goes on much longer and the country's biggest car manufacturer is considering halting production, spokesmen said on Tuesday.

Carlos Cazenave, head of the National Association for the Transport of Goods by Road (ANTRAM), told Reuters that the government had promised ANTRAM in a meeting on Monday that it would press for compensation from French authorities.
"There will be bankruptcies in many companies if the strike goes on," he said in a telephone interview.
"The Portuguese government told us it would press the French government for compensation," he added. "The government has asked us to urge our drivers not to leave Portugal."
Government officials were not immediately available for comment.
Cazenave estimated that the total daily cost of the stoppage for the 1,500 Portuguese trucks now stranded in France -- a third of the national fleet -- was about 75 million escudos ($500,000).

He said about 90 percent of Portugal's total fleet was paralysed, with up to 3,000 trucks stuck in Portugal, unable to transport their produce to destinations across Europe because they could not cross France.
Cazenave said the import and export of all kinds of produce ranging from machinery parts to shoes, textiles to electronics equipment and food, were delayed by the French strike.
The French drivers were on strike for a ninth day on Tuesday, blocking roads and petrol depots around the country in a conflict that was squeezing the economy.
The truckers are demanding wage rises, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60.

Portugal's biggest car manufacturing plant, the Ford-Volkswagen AutoEuropa joint venture, was considering halting production outright from Thursday if the French strike went on unabated, spokeswoman Carmo Jardim said.
"AutoEuropa will take a decision tomorrow afternoon," she told Reuters. "The decision will be to either reduce or halt production, depending on events in France."

She said AutoEuropa, which produces 510 passenger vans per day mainly for export to Europe, had been paying an additional 50 million escudos ($330,000) per day since November 20 to fly supplies to the plant that were normally brought by road.
She said the supplies brought by chartered aircraft included engines, transmissions and air conditioning components.

Exports from AutoEuropa, the biggest foreign investment in Portugal, located 30 miles (50 km) south of Lisbon, were not affected as most finished vehicles were transported by train and boat, Jardim said.
